overview: Rabih Fadlallah built a military state through conquest and enslavement, eventually occupying Borno in 1893. This map’s eastern polygon lies far from his later capital, Dikwa: it cannot show the full extent of his changing power.

periods.title: Campaigns in Central Africa
periods.summary: The imported starting year belongs to an era of campaigning south of Lake Chad, before Rabih occupied Borno.

periods.title: The Borno phase
periods.summary: Rabih established his capital at Dikwa after conquering Borno. French-led forces defeated him in 1900.

items.text: Rabih had served the slave-trading forces associated with Zubayr and his son Sulayman. After their defeat, he and followers moved west; commanders elected him amir in 1879. His mobile force preceded the later state centred on Dikwa.

Raiding devastated communities in southern Chad and northern Central Africa. Captured people could be forced into Rabih’s army, so military growth also meant families separated and people deprived of freedom. Resistance to French conquest does not erase these harms.

Military commanders supervised local rulers and collected resources through enlarged territorial holdings. Rabih retained some experienced Borno officials, but their room to act depended on submission to his authority.

Before the invasion, weekly markets connected farmers and townspeople through grain, milk products, fish, meat and building materials. War and neighbouring states’ blockades damaged those networks. The loss was felt in ordinary shopping and meals, not just in royal income.

Food shortages worsened by 1898. Areas such as Gujba, which escaped some destruction, became important sources of grain. An army could capture a capital quickly; rebuilding the farming that fed it was much harder.

Travelling toward Dikwa after Rabih’s defeat in 1900, Émile Gentil first mistook newly planted fields for empty plains. He then noticed channels designed to hold rainwater. The apparent emptiness was a visitor’s misunderstanding of farming.

Gentil’s June 1900 journey also records local people bringing fresh milk and butter. Millet fields and livestock supported settlements along his route. These are observations from just after the war, rather than a menu for every household.

Dikwa’s palace builders bundled smaller timbers into supporting pillars where large wood was scarce. Gentil described thick walls, several courtyards and plastered surfaces: practical engineering on a grand scale.

In the market Gentil saw local cotton alongside imported fabrics, sugar, coffee, tea and metal goods. His account describes a busy city after conquest; it does not cancel the evidence of severe wartime disruption elsewhere.

sections.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler

items.text: A letter of 28 November 1894 from al-Sanusi al-Bakr proposed trade on behalf of Rabih and the ruler of Wadai. It discussed animals, textiles and guns, but also trading enslaved people. Diplomatic paperwork exposes coercion behind the word commerce.

Writing sample: “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God,” appears in that 1894 Arabic letter’s opening. This is a normalized transcription from the published edition. The author was al-Sanusi, writing about Rabih’s trade interests; these are not words from a verified Rabih autograph.

Rabih’s death did not make his followers disappear. His son Fadlallah led a surviving force, and families moved with the defeated army. Their later negotiations and flight belong to the story too, beyond a map’s single ending date.

ending.text: Rabih died in the battle near Kousseri on 22 April 1900. Fadlallah and other survivors continued resisting and negotiating into 1901. Colonial partition followed; the peoples and communities affected by these wars continued their own histories.
